messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael was fifty-one, a school principal in a Midwestern district, when a routine flu spiraled into sepsis. For three weeks in the ICU, he lay tethered to monitors and IV lines, the antiseptic reek of alcohol wipes and hand sanitizer saturating every breath. He could not move; the doctors’ hands on his chest, the cold gel of the ultrasound probe, the repeated blood draws—these became the entire texture of his waking hours. His wife had died five years earlier, and he faced those weeks alone, the beeping machines the only voice in the room.

After discharge, Michael returned to work determined to resume his life. But the world had become a minefield of sensory triggers. The first time a janitor mopped the school hallway near his office, the faint sting of rubbing alcohol hit his nostrils, and his heart slammed. He felt his body go rigid, the same frozen helplessness he had known in the ICU bed. He could not bring the actual hospital scenes to mind—when he tried to remember details, the memory slid away—yet the emotion surged without any picture, a raw terror that left him breathless. A routine physical examination he had scheduled six months later sent him into a full-body reenactment: lying on the exam table, he felt his limbs lock, as if the sepsis had returned.

These encounters with triggers did not just activate his memory; they corroded his sense of self. After a doctor’s appointment, he would think, “I can’t trust my own body anymore. It almost killed me once, and it will again.” He felt unrecognizable to himself—the confident principal who bounded through hallways had become a man who flinched at the smell of a bandage. That negative appraisal of his own unreliability, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to any olfactory cue. That same conviction—that his body could not be trusted—kept pulling him back into the ICU, the memory surfacing each time as if to prove the verdict true. He began to notice the antiseptic scent in the school nurse’s office from three doors away, scanning hallways for it every morning.

Over the months, Michael developed a set of strategies that only deepened the cycle. Before any staff meeting or parent conference, he rehearsed what he would say, poring over talking points until he had a script, because he no longer trusted his ability to respond naturally. “I can’t rely on myself to handle an unexpected question,” he told himself. This rehearsal, while offering temporary control, left him feeling even more like a stranger inside his own skin—an actor playing a principal. He began to isolate completely, canceling dinner invitations with his few remaining friends and avoiding phone calls. The isolation reinforced his belief that he had become someone he did not recognize. When he did interact, the rehearsed conversations felt hollow, and afterward he would encounter triggers more acutely: a friend’s hand sanitizer on a desk, the alcohol smell in a church foyer. Each avoidance made the next trigger feel more dangerous.

The memory intrusions fed directly into his maladaptive strategies. When the bodily reenactment seized him—usually triggered by a hospital smell or a reminder of a procedure—he would cancel plans for the rest of the day, holing up in his office or home. “I can’t let anyone see me like this,” he thought, “because this frozen, helpless person isn’t me.” The emotion-without-image episodes were particularly disturbing; he would feel the full dread of the ICU without any story to attach it to, and then conclude, “See, your body is betraying you again.” This strengthened his resolve to avoid medical settings altogether—he had not been to a physician in eighteen months, even when a persistent cough worried him.

Now, nearly two years later, Michael stands in the threshold of his own life. A colleague recently pulled him aside and said he seemed distant, that the staff missed his easy laugh. The comment stung because it was true. He finally made an appointment with a therapist, not because he believes he can change, but because the isolation has grown unbearable. What frightens him most is the thought that the person he was is gone forever, that his body will always be an enemy. What he hopes for, barely, is to find a version of himself he can live inside without constant vigilance.
